709080.t: Etymology tree Ancient Greek μυέω (mŭéō) Proto-Indo-European *-tósder.

709003.t: From Proto-Hellenic *mónwos. The etymology of the initial element is uncertain, but it may come from a Proto-Indo-European *men- (“small”); for the ending, compare οἶος (oîos, “only, single”) from *óywos.

709018.t: Of unclear origin: * Many attempts have been made to connect it with Latin fōrma (“form”) (see there for theory of its origin), but the proposed relationship is problematic.

709049.t: Traditionally (Pokorny, Vasmer, etc.) grouped with Proto-Slavic *myslь (“idea, thought”), Lithuanian mausti (“to long for”), Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐌿𐌳𐌾𐌰𐌽 (maudjan, “to remind”), Sanskrit मिथ्या (mithyā, “false, spurious, illusory”), all of which point to…

709075.t: From Proto-Hellenic *mū́s, from Proto-Indo-European *múHs (“mouse”). Cognates include Latin mūs, Sanskrit मूष् (mū́ṣ), Old Armenian մուկն (mukn) and Old English mūs (English mouse).

709054.t: From Proto-Hellenic *mólā, from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind; crush”). Doublet of μύλος (mŭ́los).

709016.t: Traditionally derived from a Proto-Indo-European *mórom (“mulberry, blackberry”), and cognate with Old Armenian մոր (mor, “blackberry”), as well as likely Middle Irish merenn (“mulberry”), Welsh merwydden.

709070.t: From Proto-Indo-European *morwís (“ant”). Related to Old Armenian մրջիւն (mrǰiwn) and Latin formīca and perhaps Sanskrit वल्मी (valmī).

709050.t: From Proto-Indo-European *mus- (“a fly”), whence also Latin musca, Old Church Slavonic моуха (muxa), Old Armenian մուն (mun), Albanian mizë, Latvian muša, Old English mycg (English midge).

709040.t: According to Beekes, ultimately of Pre-Greek origin.

709081.t: From μυέω (muéō, “to initiate into mysteries”), from μύω (mū́ō, “to shut”), + -της (-tēs).

709039.t: Unknown. It is traditionally compared with ἄχθος (ákhthos), βρόχθος (brókhthos) and ὄχθος (ókhthos).

709072.t: A Kulturwort which spread to various other languages, of disputed origin: * Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *smer- (“to anoint, smear”), along with σμύρις (smúris, “emery”), and connected with Proto-Indo-European *smérus (“grease”) (whence…

709063.t: From μυριάς (mūriás, “number of 10,000”), from μυρίος (mūríos, “numberless, countless, infinite”).

709017.t: From o-grade of the root of μείρομαι (meíromai, “to receive as one's portion”).

709051.t: From μύσσομαι (mússomai, “to blow the nose”) + -τήρ (-tḗr). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mew-k- (“slip; slime”), the same root of μύκης (mŭ́kēs, “mushroom”), μύξα (mŭ́xă, “mucus; slime”) and Latin mucus.

709046.t: Unclear. The word has been linked with μυών (muṓn, “cluster of muscles”) because both marrow and muscles are soft in texture.

709029.t: According to Beekes, related to Old Armenian մոզի (mozi, “calf”) and maybe from a Proto-Indo-European *mosǵʰ-o- (“young of an animal; young shoot”).

709079.t: According to Beekes, both the variants listed in the alternative forms section suggest a Pre-Greek origin.

709099.t: Beekes dismisses a derivation from ὤψ (ṓps, “face”) and prefers to derive it from Pre-Greek, comparing other words ending in "-ωψ", like κύνωψ (kúnōps) and κώνωψ (kṓnōps).

709078.t: The word recalls μῖσος (mîsos, “hatred”) but remains without certain etymology. Pokorny compares Irish mosach (“shaggy, bristly”), Low German mussig (“dirty”) and Russian му́слить (múslitʹ, “to suck, beslaver”).

709084.t: The connection with Old Armenian մխեմ (mxem, “to insert; to immerse”) is obsolete and semantically doubtful.

709094.t: The following is paraphrased from the entry by Beekes in his Etymological Dictionary of Greek: Beekes finds obvious to take this verb as an intensive deverbative, suggesting that the rare forms μωκός (mōkós) and μῶκος (môkos) are actually back-formations.

709083.t: From μυέω (muéō, “to initiate into mysteries”), from μύω (mū́ō, “to shut”).

709027.t: From μόσχος (móskhos, “calf; young bull”) + -άριον (-ắrĭon, diminutive suffix).
